plot_extraction.response_text:
A radio-obsessed lawyer and cemetery trustee is hired by wealthy, devout Remington Solander to arrange an unusual provision in his will. Solander endows a station to broadcast his collection of sermons, hymns, and uplifting writings, while a permanently installed radio in his mausoleum will play those broadcasts throughout the cemetery. The equipment and wavelength must never be altered, and his heirs must maintain the tomb or lose their inheritance.

After Solander dies, the broadcasting tomb becomes a sensation, attracting visitors and greatly increasing demand for cemetery plots. The trustees expand the cemetery in anticipation of huge profits. Then the government reassigns radio wavelengths: Solander’s station moves, but his unalterable tomb receiver remains fixed on the old frequency, now occupied by a station broadcasting jazz, popular songs, comedy, and risqué jokes. Legally unable to adjust or silence the radio, the trustees watch as families remove every other body from the scandalous “jazz cemetery.” The cemetery is left deserted and worthless, with only Solander remaining in his perpetually noisy tomb.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is a first-person comic satire told in the manner of an anecdotal tall tale. Its narrator is educated enough to be a lawyer and businessman, but he is vain, irritable, acquisitive, and largely blind to his own absurdity. He presents himself as the reasonable party even while fantasising about murdering a friend over radio equipment, exploiting cemetery lots, and accepting increasingly ludicrous events as ordinary. This gap between his self-image and his behaviour creates much of the humour. Direct addresses such as “Yes, sir” and “You know the sort of program” give the narrative the conversational air of a story being told aloud to a familiar listener.

The tone combines deadpan seriousness, genial exaggeration, and escalating farce. Absurd ideas are described in sober legal, commercial, and technical language: a radio-equipped tomb, perpetual battery maintenance, exclusive loud-speaking rights, and a cemetery’s profitability are all discussed as practical business matters. The comedy depends on treating the grotesque and impossible as administratively routine. Hyperbole is frequent, from acquaintances fleeing across vacant lots to every corpse being removed from the cemetery. Violent impulses, death, religious uplift, and commercial opportunism are rendered lightly rather than grimly, producing a macabre but buoyant humour.

The plot is tightly constructed around ironic reversal. It begins with enthusiasm for a fashionable new technology, introduces Solander’s grand scheme, shows the scheme becoming a spectacular commercial success, and then destroys it through an unforeseen regulatory change. The will’s meticulous safeguards, intended to make Solander’s wishes permanent, become the precise reason the mistake cannot be corrected. The ending completes the reversal: the solemn “Talking Tomb” becomes a “Jazz Tomb,” the fashionable cemetery becomes deserted, and the supposedly unfortunate dead man is declared “the lucky man.” Foreshadowing appears in the opening editorial-like paragraph, which warns against putting radio provisions into a will, and in the narrator’s repeated emphasis on the speed and unpredictability of technological change.

The prose is plain, brisk, and highly accessible, with long narrative sentences broken up by short emphatic statements and dialogue. Repetition supplies rhythm and comic insistence: “I told him I was,” “That was so, too,” and repeated references to the fourteen volumes, the fixed wavelength, and the cemetery’s new addition keep the central absurdities prominent. Lists are used for accumulation, especially when cataloguing the will’s restrictions, the broadcast material, or the effects of the disaster. Parenthetical qualifications and self-justifying asides make the narrator sound spontaneous and defensive. Dashes, exclamations, italics or verbal emphasis, and abrupt turns such as “and then the thing happened!” imitate animated oral storytelling.

Dialogue is central to characterisation. The opening argument uses extravagant comic abuse—“lunkheaded noodle,” “pin-headed idiot,” and “half-baked lunatic”—to establish the obsessive temperament of radio enthusiasts. Solander speaks in solemn, repetitive, ceremonious phrases, contrasting his lofty ideals with the impracticality of his plan. His slow delivery is caricatured through vivid similes: his words “drip down his long chin like cold molasses,” while his eyes resemble those of “a salt mackerel.” Later, snippets of popular songs and vaudeville-style patter sharply contrast with the hymns, sermons, missionary reports, and religious poems that were meant to issue from the tomb.

The diction mixes colloquial American speech with the vocabularies of law, commerce, religion, and early radio. Expressions such as “smell a rat,” “sell like hot cakes,” “old codger,” and “went right up in the air” reinforce the informal period voice. Technical details—crystal and tube sets, “A” and “B” batteries, wavelengths, call letters, hook-ups, and loud speakers—lend plausibility while also dating the story to the early broadcasting era. Legal phrases such as “last will and testament,” “provided,” and “perpetual care and maintenance” are repeated until their solemnity becomes comic. The period style also includes topical references to prohibition, jazz, flappers, popular novelty songs, and ethnic vaudeville humour.

The story satirises technological faith, attempts to control the future, moral self-importance, commercial greed, and the instability of fashion. Solander believes radio is “imperishable,” yet its standards change almost immediately. His effort to impose uplift on posterity instead broadcasts the popular culture he despises. The cemetery trustees publicly endorse solemnity while privately calculating lot prices, publicity, and expansion. Religion, death, and memorialisation are therefore continually entangled with advertising and profit. The satire is not delivered through explicit moral commentary; it emerges from the narrator’s candid calculations and his failure to recognise how mercenary he sounds.

Imagery is concrete, caricatural, and deliberately incongruous. Solander’s “sheeplike face,” molasses-like speech, mackerel eyes, and monumental granite tomb turn him into a comic type rather than a psychologically complex figure. The final image of the emptied cemetery as a battlefield full of shell-holes pushes the consequences into surreal exaggeration. Overall, the style is that of an early twentieth-century American magazine humour piece: fast-moving, plot-driven, orally inflected, rich in comic repetition and caricature, and organised around a single ingenious premise whose logic is pursued to a disastrous punch line.

# The Permanently Tuned Tomb

If you have any property to leave when you die, put houses in your will, or bonds, or paving stock, or a red cow with one horn shorter than the other, but do not put radio in it. Radio is too lively. A house may burn, bonds may shrink, and a cow may kick the executor, but radio can alter its wavelength between breakfast and lunch and make a fool of a man before supper.

I know. I am the lawyer who drew Remington Solander’s will.

I was interested in radio myself in those days. I had a six-tube set with three dials, four batteries, a loop aerial, and a loud speaker that looked like the morning-glory trumpet Gabriel will use when the last mortgage is cancelled. It was a good set. I could get Pittsburgh, Schenectady, Chicago, Havana, and once, during a thunderstorm, something that sounded like a man drowning in Australia.

My friend Peasley said it was oscillation.

“You’re a lunkheaded noodle,” I told him. “It was Australia.”

“It was your B battery running down,” he said.

At that I took him by the collar and led him toward the back door. I am not a violent man, but nobody can insult my B battery in my own office and expect professional courtesy. Peasley grabbed my desk, upset the ink, and shouted that my hook-up had been obsolete for six months. For one instant I intended to hit him over the head with the loud speaker and bury him at Evergreen Rest Cemetery, where I happened to be a trustee and could have obtained a lot at cost. Then Miss Creel, my stenographer, came in and said Mr. Remington Solander was waiting.

So I let Peasley live.

You have probably heard of Solander. He owned the Solander Agricultural Implement Works, three flour mills, most of our traction company, and enough first mortgages to keep half the county from sleeping comfortably. He was also the most devout man I ever knew. He was devout before breakfast, devout at the office, devout while foreclosing mortgages, and especially devout when somebody else was enjoying himself.

He came into my room in a long black coat. He had a pale, sheeplike face, a narrow gray beard, and eyes like two salt mackerel laid on a plate. When he spoke, the words dripped down his chin as slowly as cold molasses.

“Mr. Tolliver,” he said, “I am informed that you understand the radio.”

I glanced at Peasley.

“I do,” I said.

Peasley made a choking sound.

“I understand it thoroughly,” I added.

“That,” said Solander, “is gratifying. It is most gratifying. Radio, Mr. Tolliver, is an imperishable voice.”

“That is so,” I said.

It was not so, of course, as things turned out, but any lawyer will tell you that a client must be allowed to state his own facts until the fee has been arranged.

“The human frame perishes,” Solander continued. “The tongue becomes dust. The lips are sealed. But radio—ah!—radio speaks on through the ages.”

“That is so, too,” I said.

Peasley sneezed into his hat.

Solander turned his mackerel eyes upon him.

“Is that person necessary?”

“Not in the slightest,” I said, and Peasley went out muttering about half-baked lunatics. He may have meant Solander. He may have meant me. Peasley was never precise in his legal terminology.

Solander then opened a black leather portfolio and laid fourteen manuscript books on my desk. They were thick books. They contained sermons he had delivered to the Men’s Moral Advancement League, addresses to the Anti-Dancing Union, reports from missionaries, prayers, admonitions, hymns, religious poems, and several essays proving that almost every modern pleasure was the first step toward ruin.

“These,” he said, touching the pile reverently, “are my message.”

“All fourteen?”

“All fourteen.”

I lifted one. It weighed four pounds.

“My purpose,” he went on, “is to establish by my last will and testament a broadcasting station. That station shall transmit, and shall transmit forever, selections from these fourteen volumes, together with approved hymns and other uplifting matter.”

“That will require an endowment,” I said.

“I have provided for an endowment of two hundred and fifty thousand dollars.”

I sat straighter. Religion is a fine thing, but an endowment makes it legally interesting.

“And now,” said Solander, “we approach the crown and summit of my purpose. I desire that my mortal remains be placed in a mausoleum at Evergreen Rest Cemetery.”

I sat straighter still. As trustee, I was entitled to be interested.

“In that mausoleum,” he said, “there shall be installed a radio receiving apparatus, with batteries, connections, aerial, amplifying tubes, and a loud-speaking horn.”

“A loud speaker in the tomb?”

“Yes.”

“To entertain you?”

He looked hurt.

“To continue my influence. The receiver shall be permanently tuned to the wavelength of my station. The programs shall issue from my mausoleum and spread over the surrounding ground. Those who come to mourn shall hear words of consolation. Those who pass idly by shall hear words of warning. Even the indifferent dead—”

He paused.

I waited.

“—will at least be in an atmosphere of righteousness,” he concluded.

This seemed fair enough. The dead at Evergreen Rest had been getting nothing but lawn mowing and rain for years.

Solander wanted the thing done properly. He was not one of those careless men who leave a nephew ten thousand dollars and neglect to say whether the nephew may spend it. No, sir. He had thought of everything.

The station must always use the same call letters. It must always transmit on precisely the same wavelength. It must use only the fourteen volumes, approved hymns, missionary reports, religious poems, and such additional matter as a board of five solemn persons might unanimously declare uplifting. No advertising was to interrupt the programs. No market reports, prize fights, dance music, jokes, recipes, election returns, or weather forecasts were to be broadcast.

The receiving set in the mausoleum must never be replaced, retuned, disconnected, repaired in any manner changing its essential character, or removed from the marble shelf on which it was first installed. Fresh A and B batteries must be supplied perpetually. Burned-out tubes could be replaced only by tubes of the identical manufacture, design, and capacity. The horn must remain pointed toward the east gate.

“Why east?” I asked.

“Most persons enter there,” he said.

That was true. Solander had considered everything.

His heirs were to receive the income from the rest of his estate, provided that they kept the mausoleum washed, the bronze doors polished, the radio operating, the batteries charged, the aerial erect, the loud speaker unobstructed, and every detail exactly as specified. Any alteration meant forfeiture. The forfeited property would go to the trustees of Evergreen Rest, of whom I was one.

I will say frankly that I liked that clause.

“What if radio changes?” I asked, merely to show foresight.

“Truth does not change,” said Solander.

“I mean the apparatus.”

“Radio is founded upon eternal scientific principles.”

Naturally, I could not argue with eternal scientific principles at my regular office rate.

It took me three weeks to draw the will. Solander read it word by word, pausing after every “whereas” as if it were a prayer. We added six codicils. One concerned lightning rods. Another required the station announcer to pronounce Solander with the accent on the first syllable. A third forbade any female vocalist whose skirts, when she stood, failed to cover the tops of her shoes.

He signed at last, and I put the will in my safe.

Eight months later Remington Solander died while dictating an address entitled “The Folly of Needless Display.”

His funeral was the largest we had ever had at Evergreen Rest. The mausoleum alone cost eighty thousand dollars. It was solid granite, with bronze doors, stained-glass windows, twelve marble columns, and a carved angel over the entrance holding one finger to its lips. That angel looked increasingly inappropriate as time went on.

The radio set was installed on its marble shelf. The aerial ran through a bronze tube to a copper wire hidden in a stone cross. The batteries stood in a ventilated chamber beneath the floor. The loud speaker, which was enormous, occupied a niche above Solander’s sarcophagus and pointed, as directed, toward the east gate.

His broadcasting station was built on Solander Hill. It had a five-hundred-watt transmitter, a studio, an organ, two announcers, a quartet, and a retired minister who could read a missionary report in a voice that made cannibalism seem unusually depressing.

At three o’clock on the first Sunday the station began.

“Good afternoon,” said the announcer. “This is station WSOL, the Voice of Solander, transmitting on three hundred and forty-one meters.”

Then the quartet sang “When the Roll Is Called Beyond the Clouds,” and the mausoleum spoke.

Yes, sir, it spoke.

The sound came out of that granite tomb as clear as if Solander himself had climbed onto the roof with a megaphone. It floated down the drives, across the flower beds, through the cedars, and over Section F, where the better class of monuments stood. People stopped. Women cried. Men removed their hats. One old gentleman, who had come to visit his third wife, dropped his cane and said he had never heard anything so improving in his life.

After the hymn, the announcer read from Volume Fourteen, “A Warning to the Frivolous Young.”

You could hear every word as far as the receiving vault.

The newspapers called it the Talking Tomb.

That name was not dignified, but it sold lots.

Visitors came by the hundreds, then by the thousands. Motorcars lined the county road. Excursion parties arrived with sandwiches. Ministers brought Sunday-school classes. Elderly ladies asked to be shown burial sites within easy hearing distance. One gentleman from Ohio bought a family lot merely because he said it would be a comfort to know where he was going to spend his radio years.

We trustees had to hire three traffic officers and a man to pick up paper bags. The refreshment privilege outside the gate brought us eight hundred dollars the first season, although naturally we condemned eating during the programs.

Demand for lots went right up in the air. Property in Section C that had lain there for twenty years at forty dollars a grave sold at one hundred and twenty-five, cash before interment. Lots nearest the mausoleum commanded a premium. We called them the Auditory Circle. That was my phrase, and I am proud of it.

The station broadcast mornings and evenings on weekdays, and continuously on Sunday except during the batteries’ rest period. At ten came sermons. At eleven came hymns. At noon came missionary news. At two there were religious poems. At four the announcer read from the fourteen volumes. At six the quartet returned, unless the tenor had one of his attacks.

The whole cemetery prospered.

We trustees began to consider expansion. Behind Evergreen Rest lay the old Kessel farm, one hundred and sixty acres of stony pasture, thistles, and discouraged apple trees. Kessel wanted seventy-five thousand dollars for it.

“Outrageous,” said Trustee Bell.

“Robbery,” said Trustee Krimp.

“Buy it,” I said.

We bought it.

We issued improvement bonds, graded drives, laid water pipes, planted six thousand young cedars, and divided the pasture into Peaceful Meadow, Celestial Terrace, Angels’ Vista, and Radio Hill. Radio Hill sold first, though it had the poorest drainage. We ordered three thousand bronze lot markers. We built a new office with a visitors’ room and a window where prospective occupants could hear WSOL before selecting their location.

Some people accused us of commercializing grief. Such people do not understand cemetery finance. Perpetual care is expensive, and a trustee must look ahead. Besides, every grave sold placed another citizen within reach of Solander’s uplifting influence. We were doing well by doing good, and doing extremely well at it.

For eighteen months nothing went wrong.

Then the government reorganized the wavelengths.

I heard about it from Peasley. He came into my office waving a newspaper.

“Well, Tolliver,” he said, “what will your dead client do now?”

“If this concerns my B battery—”

“It concerns WSOL. Under the new allocation your station moves from three hundred and forty-one meters to two hundred and seventy.”

I snatched the paper.

There it was. In order to reduce interference, improve service, separate high-powered stations, protect remote listeners, and otherwise promote the public convenience, the commission had reassigned nearly every wavelength in the country. WSOL was to move on the first of July.

“It can’t,” I said.

“It must.”

“Solander’s will says it must remain at three hundred and forty-one meters.”

“The government says two hundred and seventy.”

“Then the government has interfered with a testamentary trust.”

“The government often does worse before breakfast,” Peasley said.

I called a meeting of the trustees. We summoned the Solander heirs, the station manager, three engineers, two ministers, and Judge Wilmot, who understood wills when he was awake.

The station manager said he must obey the government or close.

The heirs said the station must continue or they would lose their inheritance.

The engineers said the mausoleum receiver could easily be retuned.

The heirs said retuning was expressly forbidden.

Trustee Bell proposed disconnecting the loud speaker.

The heirs pointed to the clause forbidding disconnection.

Trustee Krimp proposed removing the batteries.

The heirs pointed to perpetual battery maintenance.

One engineer suggested installing a second receiver inside the first receiver, but Judge Wilmot woke up long enough to say that this would be an alteration in essential character.

“Can’t we shut the tomb doors?” I asked.

“They must remain open during broadcast hours,” said the executor.

“Stuff the horn with cotton?”

“Unobstructed,” said the executor.

“Move the mausoleum?”

“Permanently situated,” said Judge Wilmot, and went back to sleep.

There was only one hopeful circumstance. Perhaps no other station would receive the abandoned wavelength.

On July first WSOL moved to two hundred and seventy meters. Its sermons, hymns, missionary reports, religious poems, and the fourteen volumes continued as before. Every radio set in the county followed it.

Every radio set except the one in Solander’s tomb.

That remained at three hundred and forty-one meters, permanently, unalterably, eternally.

For two days it gave forth nothing but static. It crackled and hissed. The angel over the door seemed to be asking for silence, but there was no silence. Still, static was not immoral. We hoped the wavelength would remain vacant.

On the third day station KJOY began broadcasting from the city.

KJOY called itself “The Pep Station.”

At nine o’clock that morning, just as a delegation from the Ladies’ Missionary Circle approached Solander’s mausoleum, the loud speaker cleared its throat with a bang and a male voice cried:

“Wake up, everybody! Shake a leg! Here come the Hot Six with ‘Kiss Me Again Behind the Kitchen Door’!”

Then the band began.

I have heard jazz before. I have even heard Peasley tune two stations at once. But I never heard such jazz as came out of Remington Solander’s tomb. There were trumpets, drums, whistles, cowbells, a banjo, and something that sounded like a cupboard full of pie tins rolling downstairs. It came out of the granite at full volume and swept across Evergreen Rest like a cyclone in a hardware store.

The Ladies’ Missionary Circle fled through Peaceful Meadow. One lost her hat in Angels’ Vista. Another crossed two vacant lots without opening the gates.

The number ended.

A young woman’s voice said, “Oh, boys, wasn’t that wicked?”

Then a comedian told a joke about a traveling salesman, a flapper, and a bottle concealed in a hot-water bag.

The Solander heirs went white.

“Turn it off!” they cried.

“We can’t,” I said.

“Retune it!”

“We can’t.”

“Do something!”

That was unreasonable. I am a lawyer, not a miracle worker.

We rushed to court. We asked permission to alter the receiver. The heirs opposed us because alteration meant forfeiture. The attorney general opposed us because the government controlled wavelengths. The station KJOY opposed us because it had obtained the frequency legally. Judge Wilmot studied the will for three weeks and decided that Solander had expressed his intentions so plainly that no court could misunderstand them, however unfortunate those intentions had become.

The tomb must continue.

And it did.

All day the proper Solander station broadcast uplifting matter on two hundred and seventy meters, while Solander himself received KJOY on three hundred and forty-one.

At ten in the morning, when WSOL aired a sermon on temperance, the tomb aired “Who Hid the Corkscrew, Rosie?”

At noon, while WSOL read a missionary report, the tomb broadcast baseball scores.

On Sunday afternoon, during Solander’s own essay against dancing, KJOY presented the Metropolitan Charleston Orchestra.

You know the sort of program. A horn would shriek, a drum would explode, and then somebody would sing:

“Clara wears her galoshes high,  
She winks at every passing guy—”

After that came jokes.

The jokes were not the worst jokes ever told, but they became worse in a cemetery. A remark that might sound merely foolish in a theater sounded criminal when shouted across six acres of tombstones.

Our lot sales stopped in one day.

Within a week families began removing bodies. The first was Mrs. Harkness. She said her husband had disliked jazz while alive and she would not have him subjected to it merely because he was helpless. Then the Pritchards removed four relatives from the Auditory Circle. Reverend Blane transferred his wife to a cemetery twelve miles away after KJOY broadcast “Oh, You Naughty Little Widow” during his memorial visit.

We tried reducing the volume, but the will required it to remain at the level fixed on the day of installation. We planted trees around the mausoleum. The sound came through them. We built an ornamental stone screen. Judge Wilmot ruled that it obstructed the loud speaker. We ran lawn mowers during the worst programs, but KJOY advertised itself as the station that could be heard above anything, and it was.

The removals became a stampede.

Every morning trucks entered Evergreen Rest carrying empty boxes. Every evening they departed with customers. Monuments came down, headstones were uprooted, family vaults were opened, and undertakers worked overtime. People who had not visited their dead for twenty years suddenly became furious about musical standards.

Our new addition suffered most. Radio Hill was cleared in nine days. Peaceful Meadow lasted two weeks. Celestial Terrace held out until KJOY introduced a midnight program called “The Pajama Frolic.” After that even the trustees removed their relatives.

I removed mine for business reasons.

By autumn Evergreen Rest looked like a battlefield. The grass was trampled, the roads were scarred, and thousands of open graves and empty foundations covered the ground like shell-holes. The office was deserted. The bronze markers rusted in a shed. The Kessel farm, for which we still owed sixty thousand dollars, was worth less than it had been when it grew thistles.

Only one body remained.

Remington Solander could not be moved, because his will forbade it.

His heirs still polish the bronze doors. They wash the granite. They replace the tubes with tubes of identical manufacture, design, and capacity. They supply fresh A and B batteries. They keep the aerial erect and the horn pointed toward the east gate. If they fail in any particular, the property comes to us trustees—and there is not enough money in the world to make me accept it.

KJOY is stronger now. It broadcasts until two in the morning.

Sometimes I drive past the old cemetery at night. Weeds cover Angels’ Vista. Rabbits live in the visitors’ room. Moonlight shines into the open holes, and from the middle of all that emptiness comes a trumpet, a laugh, a crash of drums, and some cheerful idiot shouting:

“Come on, folks! There’s life in the old place yet!”

That is why I say Remington Solander was the lucky man.

He is the only person in Evergreen Rest who cannot move away.

# The Keeper of Lost Hours

On the morning the town clock lost thirteen minutes, Mara Vale was the only person who noticed.

She stood beneath the tower in the market square, holding a paper bag of warm rolls, and watched the minute hand jump from 8:16 to 8:29. No bell rang. No gears groaned. The hand simply moved, smooth and silent, as if thirteen minutes had been erased from the face of the world.

Around her, the market continued undisturbed. Fishmongers arranged silver rows of herring. Bakers opened striped awnings. Children chased pigeons through the fountain spray. No one cried out that something impossible had happened.

Mara looked at the clock above the red roofs, then at the little brass watch in her palm.

Her watch said 8:16.

A moment later, its minute hand trembled and slid forward to 8:29.

The paper bag slipped from Mara’s fingers.

A roll bounced across the cobblestones and stopped against a polished black shoe.

“Careful,” said Mr. Quill, the town watchmaker.

He was a tall, narrow man whose gray coat always seemed too heavy for the season. He picked up the roll, brushed it with one gloved hand, and returned it to the bag.

“You saw it,” Mara said.

Mr. Quill looked toward the clock tower.

“Saw what?”

“The clock jumped.”

“Clocks don’t jump.”

“That one did.”

“Then perhaps it was startled.”

He tipped his hat and walked away.

Mara might have dismissed the incident if it had happened only once. But at noon the same day, seven minutes vanished while she was sweeping the floor of her mother’s bookshop. One instant the dust motes floated in a sunbeam near the door; the next they had shifted across the room. Her mother stood behind the counter with a cup raised halfway to her mouth.

“What happened?” Mara asked.

Her mother blinked. “What do you mean?”

“You moved.”

“I was drinking tea.”

“No, you were standing there, and then—”

The church bell rang twelve times, though Mara’s watch showed 12:07.

Her mother frowned at the clock on the wall. “That old thing must be slow again.”

By evening, everyone in Bellweather complained that the day had gone too quickly. The butcher had forgotten a delivery. The mayor arrived late to his own speech. Half the town burned its supper.

Only Mara understood that they had not forgotten anything.

Time had been stolen.

She went to Mr. Quill’s shop after sunset.

The narrow building leaned between a candle maker’s house and an abandoned tailor’s shop. Dozens of clocks crowded its window: brass carriage clocks, painted wooden cuckoo clocks, silver watches no larger than coins. Their hands pointed to different hours, yet their ticking came in perfect unison.

The door was locked.

Mara knocked.

No answer.

She knocked again, louder.

Behind the glass, every clock stopped.

The sudden silence made her step back.

Then the lock clicked, and the door opened by itself.

“Mr. Quill?” Mara called.

The shop smelled of cedar shavings and machine oil. Moonlight gleamed on hanging pendulums. Beyond the empty counter, a curtain stirred although there was no wind.

Mara should have gone home.

Instead, she stepped inside.

The door shut behind her, and all the clocks began ticking again.

She pushed through the curtain and found a workshop lined with shelves. Tiny screwdrivers lay in careful rows. Magnifying lenses hung from hooks. A green-shaded lamp burned over a half-open pocket watch.

At the far end of the room stood a blue door.

Mara knew the shape of the building. There should have been an alley beyond that wall, not another room.

She opened the door.

A spiral staircase descended farther than the cellar could possibly allow. Dim blue lamps glowed along the stone walls. From below came the steady thunder of machinery.

Mara followed the stairs down.

At the bottom, she found a chamber vast enough to contain the entire market square. Gears turned beneath a vaulted ceiling. Copper pipes twisted through the darkness. Pendulums as long as ships’ masts swung over bottomless pits.

In the center stood a machine with a hundred glass bottles arranged around a circular iron frame. Pale gold light swirled inside each bottle.

Mr. Quill was fastening a stopper into one of them.

Mara stepped closer. A paper label hung from the glass.

TUESDAY, 10:42–10:55, it read.

“You took them,” she whispered.

Mr. Quill turned. He did not look surprised.

“Thirteen minutes,” Mara said. “Then seven at noon. How many more?”

“Four at sunset,” he replied. “You were eating soup. You didn’t notice.”

“Give them back.”

“I can’t.”

“Why not?”

“Because they have already been used.”

He lifted the bottle. Inside, the golden light spun like a small storm.

“Used for what?”

Mr. Quill studied her for a long moment, then set the bottle into the machine. A pipe above it filled with light.

“Come with me.”

He led Mara across a bridge suspended between moving gears. Far below, something pulsed with a deep metallic heartbeat.

“You believe clocks measure time,” he said. “They do not. They merely persuade it to behave. Time is wild by nature. It stretches during lonely nights, shrinks during joyful afternoons, and tangles itself around memories. Long ago, keepers built this machine to draw time into a steady current.”

“You’re a keeper?”

“The last one.”

They reached a brass platform overlooking the heart of the machine. There, inside a cage of iron rings, hung a cracked crystal. Golden light leaked through the fracture.

“The Continuance,” Mr. Quill said. “It keeps the hours moving in their proper order. It is failing.”

Mara watched darkness creep along the edges of the crystal.

“So you steal minutes from people?”

“I collect moments that will cause the least harm and feed them into the machine. A wait at a quiet window. A pause between one footstep and the next. Thirteen minutes on an ordinary morning.”

“They weren’t yours to take.”

“No,” he said. “But without them, tomorrow may never arrive.”

Mara wanted to call him a liar. Then the crystal shuddered, and the chamber changed.

For one terrible instant, she saw the machine as a rusted ruin. Mr. Quill was gone. Bones lay among the gears. She saw herself standing on the platform with white hair and a wrinkled hand.

Then the vision snapped away.

“The crack is widening,” Mr. Quill said. “Soon minutes will not merely disappear. They will fall out of order. A woman may grow old before she gives birth. A house may burn before the candle is lit. Morning may follow morning forever.”

Mara gripped the railing.

“How do we repair it?”

“I have searched for forty years. The Continuance cannot be repaired from within time. Someone must enter the Unmeasured Hour.”

“What is that?”

“The space between one day and the next. A place where time has no direction.”

“Then go there.”

Mr. Quill looked toward the turning gears.

“I tried.”

He removed his right glove. His hand beneath was not flesh but clear glass, filled with drifting sand.

“The Unmeasured Hour takes time from whoever enters. I lost thirty years before reaching the gate.”

Mara remembered Mr. Quill as he had looked when she was small. He had seemed old even then, unchanged through every winter.

“How old are you?”

“One hundred and seventeen. Or eighty-seven. It depends which clock you trust.”

The Continuance groaned. A new fracture appeared in the crystal.

Mr. Quill quickly opened a valve. Light flowed from the stolen bottle into the crack, sealing it with a thin gold line.

“For tonight, that will hold,” he said. “Tomorrow I will need more.”

“How much?”

“An hour, perhaps two.”

“And the day after?”

“More.”

Mara understood. “Eventually you’ll steal whole days.”

“If necessary.”

“From whom?”

His silence answered her.

The next morning, Mara found four blank pages in the journal she kept beside her bed. She always wrote before sleeping, yet she remembered nothing after leaving the underground chamber. Her mother said she had come home at ten, eaten an apple, and gone upstairs.

Three hours had vanished.

Across town, others had suffered worse. The schoolmaster found himself standing beside the river with no memory of walking there. A baker opened her oven and discovered twenty loaves already burned. An old man named Fen claimed that his wife’s portrait had changed: she had been smiling yesterday, he insisted, but now she looked away.

Mr. Quill was no longer choosing harmless moments. The machine was hungry.

At midday, the clock tower struck fourteen times.

Then the sun stopped.

It hung above the western hills for six hours while shadows remained fixed on the ground. People gathered in the square, whispering and praying. Birds circled without landing. A child dropped a red ball, and it hovered a finger’s width above the stones.

Mara ran to the watchmaker’s shop.

The blue door stood open.

Below, Mr. Quill fought with the controls of the machine. Several bottles had shattered. Golden light poured across the floor, where it became flickering images: a first kiss, a funeral, a boy running through rain, a woman closing a garden gate.

“The Continuance has stopped,” he shouted over the grinding gears. “I can restart it, but the repair will consume every stored hour.”

“Then do it.”

“It would give us one day. No more.”

“Show me the gate.”

Mr. Quill stared at her.

“The gate to the Unmeasured Hour,” Mara said. “Show me.”

“You would not return.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I know better than anyone.”

“Then you know stealing time won’t save us.”

The great pendulums slowed. One by one, the blue lamps went dark.

Mr. Quill’s shoulders sagged.

At last, he reached beneath his coat and removed a silver key on a chain.

“The gate is below the machine,” he said. “There is a staircase beside the central gear. When you enter, hold tightly to one memory. It may lead you home.”

“What am I looking for?”

“The First Clock—the clock from which all others learned their rhythm. Its bell can call time back into order.”

“And if it doesn’t?”

“Then nothing will.”

The staircase beneath the machine ended at a door with no handle. Mara pressed the silver key against its surface. A keyhole appeared.

Behind the door lay a field of stars.

She stepped through.

There was no ground, yet she did not fall. There was no sky, yet lights burned above and below her. Around her floated pieces of unfinished moments: rain that never reached the earth, words that had not yet been spoken, tears suspended before they could fall.

Mara tried to remember the bookshop.

She pictured her mother behind the counter, sunlight in her hair. She remembered the smell of paper, dust, and tea. She held the memory as tightly as she could.

Already, other things were fading.

She could not recall what she had eaten for breakfast. She could not remember the mayor’s name. When she tried to picture her own room, she saw only a door opening into darkness.

Ahead, bells chimed.

Mara followed the sound.

She passed an army frozen on the edge of battle. She saw a city not yet built and another sinking beneath black water. She saw herself at many ages: a child laughing by the fountain, a woman holding a newborn baby, an old figure sitting alone in Mr. Quill’s shop.

“None of this has happened,” she whispered.

“Everything has happened here,” replied a voice.

A girl stood among the stars.

She looked about Mara’s age, but her eyes were ancient. Her white dress shifted from new cloth to yellowed rags and back again. In her hands she held a small wooden clock.

“Are you the keeper?” Mara asked.

“I was the first.”

“Is that the First Clock?”

“It is.”

“Give it to me.”

The girl smiled sadly. “Everyone asks for time as if it were an object to own.”

“My town is breaking apart.”

“All towns break apart. All people vanish. That is what time does.”

“Then why build the Continuance?”

“Because people were afraid. They wanted rivers to flow in one direction. They wanted children to be born before they died. They wanted promises to remain made.”

“That seems reasonable.”

“It seemed so to me, once.”

The girl lifted the wooden clock. It had no numbers and only one hand.

“The machine is failing because your keeper feeds it stolen time. Stolen time carries grief. Regret. Resentment. The Continuance was never made to consume it.”

“What does it need?”

“A gift.”

Mara thought of the bottles beneath the shop.

“How much?”

“One hour freely given.”

“That’s all?”

“Not just any hour. The hour the giver values most.”

The field of stars darkened.

Mara remembered summer evenings in the bookshop, when her mother locked the door but left the windows open. They would sit on the floor and read stories aloud while warm wind stirred the pages. There was one evening, three years earlier, when rain began suddenly. Her mother had laughed and pulled Mara into the street. They danced barefoot in the empty square while thunder rolled over the roofs.

It was Mara’s happiest memory.

She felt the Unmeasured Hour waiting.

“If I give it,” she asked, “will I forget?”

“Yes.”

“Will my mother?”

“No.”

That seemed almost crueler.

Mara closed her eyes.

She heard rain striking cobblestones. She felt her mother’s hands in hers. She saw their reflections turning in the dark shop windows.

“I give that hour,” she said.

Pain passed through her—not sharp, but hollow. A door closed somewhere inside her mind.

When she opened her eyes, she was crying, though she no longer knew why.

The girl placed the wooden clock in her hands.

“Carry it home.”

“How?”

“Follow what remains.”

Mara searched for her memory of the bookshop, but it had become faint. She saw shelves, a green door, a woman whose face she loved. It was enough.

She ran.

Stars streamed past her. Unspoken words burst like bubbles against her skin. Years pulled at her clothes. Her hands became small, then wrinkled, then young again.

In the distance, a rectangular doorway shone.

It began to close.

Mara leaped.

She landed on the stone floor beneath the machine.

Mr. Quill caught her before she struck the stairs. His hair had turned completely white, and cracks covered his glass hand.

“How long?” Mara gasped.

“For you? I cannot say. For me, nine years.”

He helped her climb to the central platform. The Continuance was almost entirely dark. Outside the chamber, the world had gone silent.

Mara held up the First Clock.

“Where does it go?”

Mr. Quill pointed to a hollow inside the cage of rings.

Mara placed the wooden clock beside the cracked crystal.

Nothing happened.

Then the clock’s single hand moved.

Tick.

The sound rolled outward like thunder.

The crystal blazed. Golden light raced through the machine, along every pipe and wire, into the foundations of the town. The pendulums swung. The gears turned. Every bottle shattered at once, releasing stolen moments in a storm of radiance.

Mara saw them rise through the ceiling.

Above, the butcher remembered his missing delivery. The schoolmaster found his lost walk beside the river. Burned loaves became dough, then baked again. The red ball dropped and bounced. Portraits shifted in their frames.

The sun plunged below the hills, then rose in the east, then settled into its proper place in the evening sky.

The clock tower struck once.

The sound traveled across Bellweather, through every house and every heart.

Time began again.

Mr. Quill sat heavily on the floor.

His glass hand had become flesh.

“It’s finished,” Mara said.

“No,” he replied, smiling. “It has begun.”

They climbed out of the underground chamber shortly before dawn.

In the market square, people wandered from their houses, confused but unharmed. Some had recovered lost minutes, others whole afternoons. A woman embraced a brother she had forgotten visiting. A child laughed because his ice cream had returned to its cone.

Mara’s mother ran from the bookshop and pulled her close.

“I thought I’d lost you.”

“I’m here,” Mara said.

Her mother held her at arm’s length. “Do you remember?”

“Remember what?”

“The rain. Three summers ago. We danced in the square, and you slipped near the fountain.”

Mara searched her mind.

There was only a warm emptiness.

“No,” she said.

Her mother’s smile trembled. “It was a good evening.”

“Tell me about it.”

So her mother did.

She told Mara how the rain had soaked their clothes, how lightning had frightened all the pigeons from the roofs, how they had laughed until they could scarcely breathe. As Mara listened, she could not recover the hour she had given away, but she could see its reflection in her mother’s face.

That, she decided, was enough.

Mr. Quill left Bellweather the following spring. He put his shop, his tools, and all his clocks in Mara’s care.

“I’m sixteen,” she protested.

“You are also the only person who noticed thirteen missing minutes.”

“Where will you go?”

“Somewhere clocks are allowed to be wrong.”

On his last morning, he handed her the key to the blue door.

“Will the Continuance fail again?” she asked.

“Everything fails eventually.”

“That isn’t comforting.”

“No,” he agreed. “But until then, it will need watching—not controlling, not feeding, merely watching.”

Mara looked up at the clock tower. Its hands pointed to 8:16.

“How will I know if something is wrong?”

“You’ll notice.”

He tipped his hat and walked toward the eastern road.

Years later, travelers came to Bellweather to have their clocks repaired by Mara Vale. They said she could hear a broken spring from across a crowded room. They said she never charged children, sailors, or anyone who arrived late to a funeral.

In her shop window, dozens of clocks ticked in imperfect harmony. Some gained a minute each week. Others lost two. Mara allowed these small errors. She had learned that time did not need to be flawless in order to move forward.

Every year, on the first summer evening when rain fell over the town, Mara’s mother closed the bookshop early.

They went into the square together.

Mara never remembered why.

But as the rain ran down her face and the clock tower rang above them, she always took her mother’s hands.

And they danced.
